splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Courts disagree on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year, or whether actuaries retain discretion to select assumptions after that date. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be determined as of the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers greater predictability about potential withdrawal liability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that plan actuaries may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing the use of updated information in calculating withdrawal liability.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund v. M & K Employee Solutions

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the supervision period beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year and raises questions about judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is tolled during the period a supervisee absconds, extending the court's authority to revoke supervised release beyond the original term.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is not tolled during absconding because no statute authorizes such tolling, and courts lack the power to extend the punishment period beyond what Congress prescribed.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: A longstanding 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether federal prisoners face the categorical bar of Section 2244(b)(1) — which prohibits raising any claim previously presented — when bringing successive collateral attacks under Section 2255. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners are categorically barred from re-raising claims; if not, they need only satisfy 2255(h)'s requirements of showing newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to Section 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the (b)(1) bar on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing under Section 2255, imposing a stricter gatekeeping requirement.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to Section 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the (b)(1) bar does not apply to federal prisoners under Section 2255, so they need only satisfy 2255(h)'s requirements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates can demonstrate a concrete injury sufficient for Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to state voting procedures like ballot-receipt deadlines. The resolution affects whether election-rule challenges can be litigated before elections take place or must wait until after, when relief may be ineffective.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate suffers a cognizable competitive injury from permissive ballot-receipt laws and therefore has Article III standing to challenge the law before an election.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate's generalized competitive concerns about election rules are insufficient to establish Article III standing absent a concrete particularized injury.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Jacobson v. Florida Secretary of State

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: A deep circuit split exists on whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief under 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1) only if they meet all three listed criminal-history criteria, or whether possessing any one of them is disqualifying. The split leads to disparate sentencing outcomes for defendants with identical criminal histories depending on geographic location.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that 'and' in § 3553(f)(1) means all three criminal-history criteria must be present to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations of ambiguous criminal provisions, or whether agency deference overrides lenity.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether courts should apply the rule of lenity or defer to agency/Sentencing Commission interpretations when criminal statutes or guidelines are ambiguous. At least three circuits hold lenity trumps deference, while the Third Circuit has held that agency deference trumps lenity, placing it on the opposite side of a circuit split deepened by Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity prevails over agency or Sentencing Commission deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal provisions, preventing agencies from using delegated power to expand criminal liability.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference takes precedence over the rule of lenity when interpreting ambiguous guidelines enhancements in criminal sentencing.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) encompasses inchoate offenses like conspiracy, based on Application Note 1 to that guideline.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which states that 'controlled substance offense' includes conspiracy, is a valid and authoritative interpretation of the guideline text, which does not expressly mention inchoate offenses. This affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy convictions qualify as career offenders under the Guidelines.

positions.label: Application Note 1 is authoritative — inchoate offenses qualify
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation entitled to deference under Stinson v. United States, and thus conspiracy and other inchoate offenses qualify as controlled substance offenses for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Application Note 1 exceeds guideline text — inchoate offenses do not qualify
positions.summary: Holds that the plain text of § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the guideline's definition, especially after Kisor v. Wilkie.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute or contribute to an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply divided on whether non-retroactive changes in law — particularly the First Step Act's elimination of mandatory consecutive stacked sentences for § 924(c) offenses — may be considered as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) attempted to resolve this, but some circuits question the Commission's authority to override their precedent.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes can contribute to extraordinary and compelling reasons
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider non-retroactive changes in sentencing law, alone or in combination with other factors, as contributing to extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot be extraordinary and compelling reasons
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether offered alone or in combination with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of an asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert their Chapter 13 case to Chapter 7 in good faith under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held it belongs to the estate, creating a split with other circuits that have held such appreciation belongs to the debtor under § 348(f)(1)(A).

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the bankruptcy estate
positions.summary: Holds that the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A), read with § 541(a)'s broad definition of estate property, means post-petition appreciation in property value belongs to the estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that under § 348(f)(1)(A), post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtor, consistent with the statute's structure, object, policies, and legislative history protecting good-faith converting debtors.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the substance is controlled under state law but not under the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the Sentencing Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) requires the substance to be controlled under federal law or whether a state-law controlled substance is sufficient. This affects whether defendants with state drug convictions for substances not on the federal schedules receive career-offender or other sentencing enhancements.

positions.label: State-law controlled substance is sufficient
positions.summary: Holds that § 4B1.2(b) broadly defines 'controlled substance offense' to include state-law offenses regardless of whether the substance is on the federal schedule, finding no textual basis to graft a federal-law limitation onto the guideline.

positions.label: Substance must be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance involved is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for an order denying attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment is governed by the civil (30/60-day) or criminal (14-day) deadline for filing a notice of appeal.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees in a criminal case is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (triggering the longer civil appeal deadline) or part of the criminal case (triggering the shorter 14-day deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies.

positions.label: Civil appeal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the civil appeal deadline (30 or 60 days) governs the time to appeal.

positions.label: Criminal appeal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment fee motion is part of the criminal case and therefore subject to the 14-day criminal appeal deadline.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging the conditions or terms of their confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) must proceed via habeas corpus or may bring civil rights claims under Bivens or other civil statutes.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for prisoners challenging conditions that affect the duration or execution of their sentences — such as BOP decisions about earned time credits or prerelease custody — or whether civil rights actions are also available. This affects how federal prisoners can challenge BOP decisions under the First Step Act and other statutes.

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive for challenges affecting duration of confinement
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner's challenge to conditions of confinement effectively seeks a speedier release, habeas corpus is the sole federal remedy, following Preiser v. Rodriguez.

positions.label: Civil rights claims also available for conditions of confinement
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to prison conditions that do not directly challenge the validity of the conviction or sentence may proceed as civil rights actions even if they incidentally affect the duration of confinement.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may consider punitive purposes when revoking supervised release and imposing a sentence upon revocation, or whether revocation sentencing must be limited to the goals of supervised release itself.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether a district court may expressly punish a defendant for violations of supervised release or whether revocation sentences must be calibrated only to the breach of trust and the need to promote the goals of supervised release. The Sixth Circuit's en banc precedent allows express punishment, placing it at the extreme of the split.

positions.label: Punishment is a permissible purpose at revocation
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release conditions when imposing revocation sentences.

positions.label: Revocation sentencing must focus on breach of trust, not punishment
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentencing should be calibrated primarily to the breach of the court's trust and the defendant's need for supervision, not to punish the defendant for the underlying violation conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which bars states from enacting or enforcing laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any . . . broker,' preempts state negligence claims arising from a freight broker's selection of a motor carrier. This question affects liability in the trucking industry where brokers play a significant intermediary role.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted because they relate to the broker's 'service' of arranging transportation, which falls within the FAAAA's preemption clause.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers for negligent hiring of motor carriers are not preempted because they do not directly regulate brokers' prices, routes, or services within the meaning of the FAAAA.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to a person who uses marijuana.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass'n v. Bruen, circuits have split on whether the federal prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users — particularly marijuana users — is consistent with the Second Amendment's text and historical tradition of firearms regulation.

positions.label: § 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) does not violate the Second Amendment because the historical tradition of firearms regulation supports disarming individuals whose drug use renders them dangerous or irresponsible.

positions.label: § 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a sufficient historical analogue justifying the disarmament of non-violent drug users.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence — claims that might also be raised in a habeas petition under Section 2255 — as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under Section 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether claims that could be raised in a § 2255 habeas petition — such as alleged legal errors in a conviction or sentence — can also be considered as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A). Some circuits permit such consideration, while others hold that compassionate release cannot be used as a substitute for habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors in compassionate release analysis
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider potential legal errors in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis, as there is no categorical bar on such consideration.

positions.label: May not use compassionate release to address habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that claims challenging the legality of a conviction or sentence belong in a § 2255 motion and cannot serve as the basis for compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments under 42 U.S.C. § 1981?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to address the Second Circuit's approach to discrimination claims in the hospitality industry, indicating an unsettled or split legal framework regarding the standards for establishing discrimination liability and available remedies when patrons allege unfair treatment by business operators.

positions.label: Second Circuit approach
positions.summary: Applied certain standards for evaluating discrimination claims against hospitality establishments that the Supreme Court found sufficiently important or unsettled to warrant review.

positions.label: Other circuits' approach
positions.summary: Other circuits have applied different or conflicting standards for evaluating discrimination claims under § 1981 in the context of service and hospitality establishments.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the Section 1 exemption for transportation workers, particularly whether last-mile delivery workers who distribute goods to retail stores are 'engaged in . . . interstate commerce.' This affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a wide range of distribution workers.

positions.label: Broad exemption — last-mile delivery workers qualify
positions.summary: Holds that workers who are part of a continuous interstate transportation chain, including those making last-mile deliveries of goods that have moved in interstate commerce, qualify as transportation workers exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow exemption — last-mile distributors do not qualify
positions.summary: Holds that distribution workers delivering goods locally to retail stores are not 'transportation workers engaged in . . . interstate commerce' under Section 1 because they are not themselves moving goods across state lines.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claims are based on labeling that the EPA approved. This affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticides nationwide.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would require labeling different from or in addition to what the EPA has approved.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because they impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements, consistent with the Supreme Court's Bates v. Dow Agrosciences framework.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA creates a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits have held that RLUIPA, enacted under the Spending Clause, does not clearly authorize personal-liability damages against individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds, while others have allowed such claims to proceed.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA provides a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials sued in their individual capacities for violations of prisoners' religious exercise rights.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials because Congress cannot impose personal liability on non-recipient individuals through the Spending Clause.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
